spoken: Independent comparisons ask how separate groups differ on the same outcome. Each participant belongs to one group. Here, the scores are simulated performance points.
The menu connects descriptives, assumptions, test results, effect sizes and power analysis.
Within each view, the controls change the method or the display. We'll look at the groups, interpret their difference, and then ask what a future study would need.
Group B averages six points higher than Group A. Each group has thirty scores, and the spread in each is about ten points.
The box plot shows how much those distributions overlap. An average difference still leaves a lot of shared variation.
Welch's test compares the group means without requiring the variances to be equal.
The diagnostic note says the spreads look similar, and it points toward a shape check instead of running one on this screen. That supports judgment. It does not choose the test.
The estimated difference, Group A minus Group B, is minus six points. The interval describes the uncertainty around that estimate.
Hedges g puts the same difference on the scale of the variation. Here it is a medium effect. Statistical significance is a separate decision from the size of the difference.

Power planning asks what a future study would need. This planner uses a noncentral F model for two groups. For a hypothetical eta-squared of zero point zero eight three, about a standardised difference of zero point six, and eighty percent power, it calls for eighty-nine participants in total.
A smaller difference, eta-squared zero point zero three eight, needs a larger study: two hundred and one participants.

With that first planning assumption and the sixty people already observed, the same model gives about sixty-three percent power. That describes a future study. It is not evidence that this result is true.
A rank-based comparison gives another view of the same scores. It asks whether the distributions differ, which is not the same question as a difference in means.
